Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $S\subseteq M$ is an embedded submanifold, then the normal bundle
$\nu(S)=TM|_S/TS$ and the conormal bundle $N^*S\subseteq T^*M|_S$ are smooth
vector bundles over $S$.

Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedding, and suppose its normal bundle
$\nu(S)$ ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]) has
been equipped with its standard smooth-vector-bundle structure. Under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the existence of this structure is supplied by
[[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]].

A **tubular neighbourhood of $S$ in $M$** consists of:

1. an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq \nu(S)$ of the zero section, and
2. a smooth embedding $\Phi:\Omega\to M$

such that:

- $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$, and
- $\Phi(\Omega)$ is an open neighbourhood of $i(S)$ in $M$.

Equivalently, $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism from $\Omega$ onto an ambient open
neighbourhood of $S$, and its restriction to the zero section is the original
inclusion.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $S\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded submanifold, let $
u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(
u(S))$ whose restrictions to the zero section are the inclusion of $S$ ([[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Assume that $d\Phi_1$ and $d\Phi_2$ induce the same isomorphism from each vertical fibre $
u(S)_p$ to the ambient normal quotient $T_pN/T_pS$. (The usual normalization makes both induced maps the identity; merely fixing the zero section is insufficient.) Then, after shrinking $\Omega$ around the zero section, the two embeddings are isotopic through tubular neighbourhood embeddings fixing $S$ pointwise. Consequently, for every compact $A\subseteq S$ there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, compact support, $H_t\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$ (in particular $H_1\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_2$ there), and $H_t$ fixing a neighbourhood of $A$ in $S$ pointwise; when $S$ is compact one may take $A=S$ and obtain the agreement on a neighbourhood of all of $S$, with support in any prescribed neighbourhood of $\Phi_1(\Omega)\cup\Phi_2(\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be an
oriented smooth embedded circle and let $s$ be a smooth nowhere-zero section of
its normal bundle. For any tubular neighbourhood chart that is the inclusion
on the zero section and identifies each vertical normal fibre with the ambient
normal quotient by the identity, the curve $K_{\varepsilon s}$ obtained by
mapping the graph of $\varepsilon s$ into $S^3$ is an embedded oriented circle
disjoint from $K$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. The integer
linking number of $K$ with $K_{\varepsilon s}$ is independent of the sufficiently
small radius, of the representative section in its homotopy class, and of the
normalized tubular chart. It therefore defines a self-linking integer of the
framing class $[s]$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The zero section of $\nu K$ is compact, so after shrinking the parameter interval there is a $\delta>0$ such that $\rho(t,\varepsilon):=\pi\Phi(K(t),\varepsilon[b_D(t)])$ is smooth on $S^1\times(-\delta,\delta)$, with $\rho(t,0)=\gamma(t)$. The normalized-chart condition says that $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ represents $R\widehat T_\gamma(t)$ modulo the tangent line spanned by $\gamma'(t)$. Therefore $\gamma'(t)$ and $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ are linearly independent at every $t$. By [F4], $(t,\varepsilon)\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective near every $(t,0)$. Compactness of $S^1$ and [F7] give an open diagonal neighbourhood $V_\Delta\subseteq S^1\times S^1$ and a uniform $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that, for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, whenever $(s,t)\in V_\Delta$, the points $\rho(s,0)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, and the points $\rho(s,\varepsilon)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, lie in one common injectivity chart. Shrink $V_\Delta$, if necessary, so that it contains no off-diagonal crossing pair; this is possible because there are finitely many such pairs. Hence there are no projected coincidences between the original and offset branches with close parameters, and $t\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective. Choose disjoint small open neighbourhoods of the finitely many ordered crossing pairs of $\gamma$ outside $V_\Delta$; by [F1], these are the only off-diagonal equalities $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$. The compact complement of $V_\Delta$ and those crossing neighbourhoods contains no such equality, so $\lVert\gamma(s)-\gamma(t)\rVert$ has a positive minimum there. Smoothness gives uniform convergence $\rho(\cdot,\varepsilon)\to\gamma$, excluding original/offset and offset/offset projected coincidences on this compact complement for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Thus every projected coincidence lies in one of the chosen crossing neighbourhoods.

Fix one crossing disk with disjoint parameter intervals around the over branch $\alpha$ and under branch $\beta$, and with no other branch entering. For $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, the map $$G_{ij}(s,t,\varepsilon):=\bigl(\rho(s,i\varepsilon)-\rho(t,j\varepsilon),\varepsilon\bigr)$$ has invertible derivative at the original crossing and $\varepsilon=0$: its first two columns are $\alpha'(0)$ and $-\beta'(0)$, which are linearly independent by transversality, and its last coordinate is $\varepsilon$. By [F4], each of the four branch pairs has exactly one transverse projected intersection near this crossing for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. They are, respectively, the original crossing, the two mixed crossings, and the crossing of the two offset branches. The local injectivity from step 1.1 excludes intersections between an original branch and its own offset; it also implies that the four listed crossing points are distinct, since a coincidence between any two would place an original branch and its own offset at the same projected point. Thus there are no triple points in this crossing disk. The strict height order of $\alpha$ over $\beta$ at the original crossing persists for all four nearby crossings when $\varepsilon$ is small. The projected tangent determinants are nonzero and vary continuously, so both mixed crossings have sign $\operatorname{sgn}(c)$ by [F2].

There are finitely many crossing disks, so choose $\varepsilon$ below all local bounds from steps 1.1 and 2.1. By [F6], the spatial push-off is an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. The projection of $K\cup K_\varepsilon$ has only the finitely many transverse double points described above and no triple points, so it is a regular diagram. Each original crossing disk contributes exactly two mixed crossings, both with the original sign, and step 1.1 excludes all other mixed crossings. Countable Choice is used only through [F6] for the tubular push-off; the finite projected-crossing argument uses no choice.
